title: The history of firefly light
tagline: 350 years from glowing wood in an air pump to a gene that lights up labs, and a race to keep the real fireflies flashing.
intro: People have always wondered how a little beetle can make light without fire. An air pump showed the glow needs air, a hot and a cold extract split it into a fuel and an enzyme, and ATP and oxygen explained the chemistry. Then came flash codes, liars, synchrony and the luciferase gene, and today scientists are counting the fireflies before they fade.

eras.name: Light that needs air
eras.summary: An air pump shows that living light goes out without air.

eras.name: The chemistry of cold light
eras.summary: Scientists split the glow into luciferin and luciferase, add ATP and oxygen, and solve luciferin's structure.

eras.name: Codes, liars and synchrony
eras.summary: Field biologists decode flash languages, find fireflies that lie, and mathematicians explain how thousands flash in time.

eras.name: Genes and switches
eras.summary: The luciferase gene is copied and put to work, the oxygen switch is explained, and the efficiency is measured again.

eras.name: Counting and protecting
eras.summary: Experts rank the threats, festivals face hard questions, and India publishes its first firefly checklist.

events.title: Glowing wood goes dark without air
events.text: Boyle put a piece of glowing rotten wood, and later glowing fish, into the glass jar of his air pump. As the air was pumped out the light faded, and when air was let back in it returned. His report reached the Royal Society on 28 November 1667 and was printed in 1668.
events.why: It was the first experiment to show that living light needs something in the air, which we now know is oxygen.

events.title: Light and air in print
events.text: Boyle's 'New experiments concerning the relation between light and air (in shining wood and fish)' appeared in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, listing his experiments with the air pump.
events.why: Other scientists could now repeat the test for themselves.

events.title: Two parts to the glow
events.text: Dubois made two extracts from the light organs of the glowing click beetle Pyrophorus. A cold-water extract glowed and faded; a boiled one never glowed; mixed together they glowed again. Sources date this work to the mid-1880s (attributed 1885).
events.why: It showed that bioluminescence needs a heat-proof fuel and a heat-sensitive helper.

events.title: Luciferin and luciferase named
events.text: Studying the glowing rock-boring clam Pholas dactylus, Dubois called the heat-stable fuel luciferin and the heat-sensitive part luciferase, after Lucifer, 'light bringer'. Some sources put the names two years earlier.
events.why: The names are still used for every glowing living thing, from fireflies to deep-sea fish.

events.title: ATP lights up a spent extract
events.text: McElroy found that firefly lantern extracts that had stopped glowing lit up again when ATP was added. ATP turned out to prime the luciferin, while the light's energy comes from its reaction with oxygen.
events.why: It tied firefly light to ATP, the energy molecule of every cell, and later made luciferase a way to measure ATP.

events.title: Almost every molecule makes a photon?
events.text: Seliger and McElroy measured the quantum yield of the firefly reaction and reported a value close to one: about 88 photons for every 100 luciferin molecules, as later papers quote it.
events.why: For nearly 50 years fireflies were called almost perfectly efficient light makers.

events.title: Luciferin's structure solved and made
events.who: Emil White, Frank McCapra, George Field and William McElroy
events.text: Chemists worked out the structure of firefly luciferin, two joined rings with a sulphur-containing ring at one end, and made it in the laboratory.
events.why: Synthetic luciferin is what ATP tests and biology labs use today.

events.title: The lantern under the electron microscope
events.text: Smith described the lantern of Photuris pennsylvanica in fine detail: light cells in rosettes round air-tube cylinders, and nerve endings on the air-tube cells rather than on the light cells.
events.why: It set up the puzzle of how a nerve can switch on cells it never touches.

events.title: Femmes fatales
events.text: Lloyd reported that predatory Photuris females copy the flash answers of other species' females, lure their males and eat them. Switching his own flash pattern, he found the same females could answer other species' codes.
events.why: It revealed lying in light, a classic case of aggressive mimicry.

events.title: Flash codes catalogued
events.text: Lloyd's study of Photinus fireflies described each species' flash pattern and the female's answer delay. The common eastern firefly male flashes about every 5.9 seconds.
events.why: Flash codes became a way to tell species apart in the dark.

events.title: How whole trees flash in time
events.text: The Bucks studied male Pteroptyx fireflies that gather in mangrove trees in Thailand and flash together, about once every 0.56 seconds, within about 20 thousandths of a second of each other. They argued each insect adjusts its own internal rhythm to the flashes it sees.
events.why: It turned a travellers' tale into a problem for biology and, later, mathematics.

events.title: A model of falling into step
events.text: Kuramoto wrote down a simple model of many oscillators, each with its own rhythm, nudging one another. Above a certain coupling strength they suddenly synchronise.
events.why: Researchers later used it for fireflies, heart cells and power grids.

events.title: The luciferase gene is copied
events.who: Jeffrey de Wet, Keith Wood, Donald Helinski and Marlene DeLuca
events.text: The team copied the luciferase gene from the lantern of the common eastern firefly, Photinus pyralis, and got bacteria to make working luciferase that glowed when given luciferin and ATP.
events.why: Luciferase could now be made to order and put into other living things.

events.title: A tobacco plant that glows
events.who: David Ow, Keith Wood, Marlene DeLuca and colleagues
events.text: The team put the firefly luciferase gene into tobacco plants. Given luciferin, the plants glowed, and a photograph of a glowing tobacco plant went around the world.
events.why: It launched luciferase as one of biology's favourite reporter genes.

events.title: Proving fireflies must synchronise
events.text: Mirollo and Strogatz proved that identical oscillators that kick each other only when they fire, as fireflies do with flashes, always end up in step.
events.why: It gave firefly synchrony a firm mathematical footing.

events.title: Synchronous fireflies in the Smokies
events.text: Naturalist Lynn Faust told scientists that the fireflies near her family cabin flashed together. Experts confirmed it: Photinus carolinus makes bursts of five to eight flashes, then about eight seconds of darkness.
events.why: It showed synchronous fireflies live in the Americas too, and the park now limits viewing by lottery.

events.title: A firefly show in Anamalai
events.text: News reports say scientists first noticed a mass, possibly synchronous, firefly display in the Anamalai Tiger Reserve in 1999 and again in 2012. Species identified there include Abscondita perplexa. The date comes from press reports, not a published paper.
events.why: It suggests India has its own spectacular congregations still waiting to be studied.

events.title: Nitric oxide flips the switch
events.text: Fireflies given nitric oxide gas with oxygen glowed, and chemicals that soak up nitric oxide blocked the flash. The team proposed that nerve signals make nitric oxide, which briefly blocks the mitochondria so oxygen can reach the light-making granules.
events.why: It is still the leading explanation of how fireflies switch their light on and off.

events.title: Oxygen is the gate
events.text: Fireflies kept in extra oxygen glowed nonstop, whether or not they normally flashed. The team concluded the lantern is kept dark by holding back oxygen.
events.why: Every model of the flash now starts with oxygen.

events.title: 41%, not 88%
events.text: Using a new instrument that counts every photon, a Japanese team measured the firefly reaction's quantum yield at 41.0 ± 7.4%, less than half the old figure, and showed how acidity turns the light red.
events.why: Firefly light is still excellent, but no longer 'nearly perfect'.

events.title: The mirror is made of uric acid
events.who: Kok-Sing Goh, Chia-Wei Li and colleagues
events.text: Studying the Taiwanese firefly Luciola cerata, the team found the lantern's white reflector layer packed with round granules of uric acid about 700 nanometres across, and showed that the layer reflects the light.
events.why: It explained how the lantern bounces its light outwards.

events.title: Testing the nitric oxide idea
events.who: Hajime Ohtsuki, Masakado Kawata and colleagues
events.text: Comparing Japanese fireflies, the team found the gene for making nitric oxide active in lanterns of a species that does not flash, and no higher in adults that flash faster. They concluded their data did not support the nitric oxide model.
events.why: The leading model of the flash switch is still being tested.

events.title: Fireflies under threat
events.text: Firefly experts around the world ranked the threats they see: habitat loss first, light at night second and pesticides third. In East Asia and South America, light pollution came first.
events.why: It gave conservation a priority list for some 2,000 firefly species.

events.title: Festivals under the spotlight
events.who: Botanists, forest officers and festival organisers
events.text: Reports from Bhandardara, Purushwadi and other Western Ghats villages listed the harm from crowds: torches and phones, crushed females, night camping and fireflies caught in bottles. Kolhapur's forest department stopped gatherings in the forest after 10 pm.
events.why: Firefly tourism can help villages, but only if it protects the fireflies.

events.title: India counts its fireflies
events.who: Parvez, Akshay Kumar Chakravarthy, Oliver Keller, Devanshu Gupta and Amlan Das
events.text: The first full checklist of India's fireflies listed 92 species in 27 genera. About 61% are found only in India, the Western Ghats has the most, and more than 50 species have not been recorded since they were first described.
events.why: It is the starting point for protecting India's fireflies.

facts: A firefly is a beetle, not a fly. There are more than 2,000 species.
Out of every 100 luciferin molecules that react, about 41 make a photon of light.
Male common eastern fireflies flash about every 6 seconds; their females answer about 2 seconds later.
Some Photuris fireflies fake other species' replies to lure and eat their males.
India has at least 92 firefly species, about 6 in 10 found nowhere else.
